highlights.content: ![]() ![FinanceWire](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/financewire--theme-light.svg) ![FinanceWire](https://s3.tradingview.com/news/logo/financewire--theme-dark.svg) # Businesses Are Starting to Pay for AI Agents: 4 Stocks Building in the Space (CHGA, META, CRM, NOW) ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/avalon-globocare.svg) ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/meta-platforms.svg) ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/salesforce.svg) ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/servicenow.svg) **Naples, Florida, USA, November 2nd, 2026, FinanceWire** Agentic AI has moved out of the demo stage and into earnings reports. Over the past few months, some of the biggest names in tech have started reporting revenue, customer counts, and usage figures tied to AI agents that answer customers, book appointments, resolve support tickets, and complete sales on their own. One of the largest enterprise software companies now reports more than $1.5 billion in annual recurring revenue from its agent platform, and the largest social media company says more than 2 million businesses use its business agent every week. Smaller companies are building in the same space, including microcaps developing agentic tools aimed directly at small businesses. Several software developers and enterprise platforms are actively building and monetizing agentic AI solutions: **Change Agents Corporation** [![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/avalon-globocare.svg)CHGA](/symbols/NASDAQ-CHGA/) is a developer of agentic AI software, building subscription-based tools that help small businesses, brands, and content creators grow revenue, get found online, and automate content creation. ![](https://s3-symbol-logo.tradingview.com/avalon-globocare.svg) The company runs its commercial AI business through its wholly owned subsidiary, Avalon Quantum AI, LLC, and its current portfolio includes Beacon, an AI search optimization platform, and Catch-Up, an autonomous AI content creation platform. Change Agents recently announced the commercial launch of Beacon, a subscription-based agentic generative search optimization platform designed to help small businesses improve their visibility across five leading AI assistants: ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Grok, and Claude. The platform deploys an AI agent that reviews a business's online presence, customer reviews, reputation, and AI visibility, then gives the owner recommendations to improve how the business shows up in AI-generated answers. Beacon starts with a free AI visibility audit that runs in five minutes or less and measures how often AI assistants recommend a business compared with its major competitors across roughly 100 common customer queries. For $20 per month, subscribers receive monthly reports, can refresh their results as often as they want, and have the option to hire Beacon's services team to carry out the recommended changes. The company is initially targeting an estimated 5.6 million U.S. small businesses with fewer than 50 employees. “AI is fundamentally changing how consumers discover businesses, yet most small business owners have little visibility into whether their companies are being recommended by AI assistants,” said Michael Mathews, Director of Change Agents Corp. The company also completed Phase 2 development of Catch-Up, its agentic AI video studio, in collaboration with Caylent, an Amazon Web Services Premier Tier partner, with funding from an AWS grant. Catch-Up is designed to let podcasters, social media influencers, and other content creators generate personalized short-form videos for multiple platforms with minimal technical expertise. Change Agents has also been accepted into the Seagate Partner Program, which gives the company access to Seagate's partner portal, including product information, training, and sales and marketing tools. Essentially, the performance of these models increasingly depends less on the compute capability of a processor – how fast the chip can calculate – and more on how quickly the chip can feed data to the calculation. It’s an issue that affects both the performance of the AI model as well as the cost for running the AI workloads. Qualcomm outlined two strategies that are widely used – one that houses the AI model in fast on-chip memory, and another that uses stacked high-bandwidth memory (HBM) to support a processor. Qualcomm advocates a third strategy – near-memory computing, or HBC – that moves the computer closers to [the all-important memory](https://www.nextplatform.com/store/2026/10/08/memory-is-the-lynchpin-of-the-it-industry-and-doubly-so-for-ai/5301841). NEXTPLATFORM AD Executives argue that to close a widening gap – to remove the memory wall – between the need for more compute and the ability to feed that demand with data, the compute needs to move closer to the memory and the data it holds. It gives the AI model faster access to the data it needs, and reduces the time, energy, and cost that come when the data needs to travel a longer distance to get to the compute. It’s an argument Qualcomm made in July when first pitching the HBC architecture, and one they continue to make now. “In traditional computer architecture, you usually have DDR, you have memory of package, you have usually plenty of capacity on that, but you have a narrow link, which moves the data very slowly,” Gerardo Giaretta, vice president and general manager of datacenter CPU and AI at Qualcomm, recently told journalists and analysts. “So far, AI has been really focusing on the HBM architecture. It basically increases the number of lanes and how fast you can move the data between the compute and the HBM. The scheme targets startups founded within the past five years that have raised less than USD $15 million. Participants will receive 12 months of free access to Firefly Pro Plus, Acrobat Studio, which includes Adobe Express Premium, and Semrush. Adobe is positioning the offer around branding, content creation and customer acquisition at a stage when founders are often handling design, marketing and sales themselves. Alongside software access, the programme includes workshops and other opportunities to learn from Adobe specialists and connect with other founders. **What is included** Firefly Pro Plus is Adobe's generative AI product for image, video and audio work. Acrobat Studio combines PDF tools, Adobe's AI Assistant and Adobe Express, while Semrush adds search and marketing data intended to show how a business appears online across both conventional and AI-led search. The package is designed to bring together content creation, document tools and marketing support in one programme for small teams. Adobe serves a wide range of customers, from individual creators and small businesses to large corporate users. The launch comes as software groups seek to embed AI more deeply into products aimed at smaller businesses and startup teams, which often work with limited budgets and staff. For early-stage companies, branding and customer communication can be difficult to prioritise when product development and fundraising take precedence. **Startup examples** Adobe highlighted several startup users as examples of the businesses it wants to reach through the programme. DataCurve, which works on fan identity and intelligence for sports, media and entertainment organisations, already uses Firefly for creative work and sees broader potential for Adobe tools in linking customer data with content creation. "Creativity is far more powerful when you understand who you're creating for. We already use Adobe Firefly for creative assets, and we see an even bigger opportunity to bring DataCurve's fan intelligence directly into the creative process. Imagine a global soccer club creating content that evolves throughout the season as it learns more about what each fan cares about. Adobe for Startups gives us the tools to start bringing that vision to life," said Aman Johar, Co-founder and CEO of DataCurve. Gondola, which is building a digital credit and portfolio system for the social media and digital content sector, said Adobe's products have been part of its workflow since the company's earliest stages. "Adobe has been part of how we work from day one. When you're launching a company, how you show up matters as much as what you build. Version 0.37 of [LLM](/dossier/llm), the command-line tool and Python library, is now available. It introduces new models, a command to add [OpenAI](/dossier/openai)-compatible endpoints, and an evolution of embeddings. The maintainer also details how they manage the influx of AI-assisted pull requests. ## Twelve Corrections Integrated and AI-Assisted Sorting Version 0.37 of [LLM](/glossaire/llm) incorporates corrections proposed by 12 authors, most of whom the maintainer indicates were assisted by AI. They specify that the review workload was less than expected and that they treat these proposals as bug reports accompanied by examples, sometimes accepting them or applying their own corrections. To sort these contributions, they rely on Opus 5.5 or [GPT](/glossaire/gpt)-6 Astra to identify the most useful fixes. While many open-source project maintainers report an influx of AI-generated pull requests, the LLM lead believes their project is the most affected among theirs, without it being a problem. Twelve contributors are explicitly thanked for this version: 0d00ciallo0721, ac1982, Allen Flux, Bian Yuhan, Bishop Kammeraad, Chen Yufeiyang, Christopher Krah, Ethan Stoner, Jiachen Xie, Olamide Faniyan, Sharat Chandra Sai Boddu, and nosmile99. A new command, llm openai endpoint add, simplifies the configuration of additional models via OpenAI-compatible endpoints. ## New Default Model and More Flexible Embeddings The default model is now gpt-6-luna, which is priced at half that of the previous default model, gpt-5.6-luna. Different colors represent clusters of data that have similar effects on learning, and different shapes within the same color represent specific data types within each cluster. Credit: KAIST") Can AI fine-tuning that once took 10 hours be completed in just three hours? KAIST researchers have developed a technology that selects the most useful training data and distributes it evenly across multiple GPUs. By reducing repetitive learning of similar data, the method shortened training time by up to 69.6% while maintaining nearly the same AI performance. The technology is expected to help develop AI tailored to specific tasks, such as corporate customer service or assisting medical professionals with information retrieval, more quickly and at lower cost. A research team led by professor Jae-Gil Lee from the School of Computing developed "CluSTER," a large language model fine-tuning technology that groups and selects data with similar effects on learning and distributes them evenly across multiple GPUs. The research findings were presented in October 2026 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026) and are available on the *arXiv* preprint server. Hyunjin Kim, a doctoral student in the KAIST School of Computing, participated in the [study](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.12584) as the first author, with Lee as the corresponding author. Youngeun Nam, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Toronto, and Jaemin Han and Wonhyeok Choi, master's students at the KAIST Graduate School of Data Science, participated as co-authors. ## Random allocation repeats similar learning A large language model must be trained further on relevant data before it can be used in a specific field such as coding or medicine. AI Agents.content: # When AI agents agree on the data but not what it means Presented by SAP Enterprise AI agents that share the same data can still make conflicting decisions because raw data rarely captures the business context — the processes, policies and priorities that determine what that data means to the company. As agents take on more decision-making, those gaps in context become harder to contain. Three problems emerge when multiple agents act without shared business semantics: identical figures lead different functions to different conclusions, agents that work correctly on their own combine into the wrong outcome, and accuracy degrades as data accumulates. Enterprises have spent years loading ever more records into central data platforms, separating them in the process from the policies, processes and business context where they originated. That separation is at the root of the problem, says Irfan Khan, president and chief product officer for SAP Data & Analytics. “If you access data from a source environment and it doesn’t have the context, the likelihood is you’re going to make an ill-informed decision,” he explains. "Users learn from history only when institutional knowledge helps them separate signal from noise. An agent starts with no such knowledge unless the company supplies it." ## The agent coordination gap in multi-agent AI systems Traditional data strategies extract records from source systems and centralize them, which separates the data from the semantics and process context it carried at the source. The shift toward separating storage and compute let companies scale each independently and encouraged many to build multiple data lakes alongside on-premises estates, flat files and object stores, leading to fragmented data increasingly separated from its original business context. In multi-agent systems, missing context doesn’t stay a data problem. Once agents divide a business process among them, it becomes a coordination failure. For instance, a procurement agent negotiates longer payment terms to improve margins, a treasury agent delays payments to preserve liquidity, and a compliance agent holds payments until every validation clears. Each one is performing its assigned job correctly, but together they're stalling supplier payments long enough that critical vendors start deprioritizing the company, and no internal system flags anything as broken. Plus, few business processes run on a single agent from end to end. An order entry agent might hand off to one that checks inventory, which hands off to another that files a procurement request or decrements stock. If those steps run out of sequence, one agent can decrement an account before another has confirmed the goods exist, and the task can be completed, but the outcome can still be wrong. And there's no reason agents would coordinate any better than people do when nobody manages the handoffs, Khan says. “It’s almost like pushing out a task to 20 individual people to go and get it done for a client, and then you realize that nobody held a team meeting,” he says. “Nobody kept an inventory of where you were, or where you are within the process.” ## A business data fabric gives agents shared business context Giving agents access to distributed enterprise data solves only part of the problem. They also need a common understanding of how the business expects that data to be interpreted and acted upon. SAP’s business data fabric architecture is designed to preserve that meaning as data moves across systems rather than separating it from its original business context. It connects data and its semantics with the processes, policies, and other business knowledge that govern how the data is used, while allowing agents to reach information across distributed environments. AI Agents.titleZh: Unifying Data Context Is Essential to AI Agents' Success - Business Insider
AI Agents.content: By Manish Sood, founder & CEO of Reltio, an SAP company, and Irfan Khan, president & chief product officer of SAP Data & Analytics Sixty-three percent of organizations either lack or aren't sure they have the data management required for AI, according to Gartner. Worse, the firm predicts that companies will abandon 60% of AI projects by the end of this year due to a lack of AI-ready data. Not because of model performance, talent, or cost. It's the data they already have but can't use. Across every industry, enterprises are deploying autonomous AI agents to execute workflows and make decisions at machine speed. Yet the data those agents rely on remains fragmented, duplicated, and inconsistent. The agent isn't the bottleneck — the scattered data layer underneath it is. Before AI agents can deliver meaningful ROI, organizations must bridge the gap between content and context. Otherwise, they risk automating ambiguity at unprecedented speed. Ask a large organization how many active customers it has, and sales, finance, and support will each cite a different number. None of them is necessarily wrong. They simply never agreed on what "active" means in the first place. When a human employee spots a data discrepancy, they ask a colleague for context. An AI agent does not. Unless explicitly programmed to flag ambiguity, an agent will instantly select an answer and act on it across enterprise systems. That speed makes agents valuable, but also dangerous. An agent acting on an incorrect definition of "active customer" doesn't just produce a flawed spreadsheet; it triggers misrouted shipments, duplicate outreach campaigns, or unnecessary compliance flags. The errors compound before human oversight can intervene. The consequences of bad data aren't new, but the speed at which they now play out is. When this problem surfaces, the typical executive instinct is to consolidate and move everything into a single data lake or platform. But consolidation merely puts conflicting records in the same room. It doesn't resolve which record is accurate, how the records relate, or what "active customer" means in a specific workflow. Consolidation gathers data in one place. Unification resolves identity, establishes shared definitions, maps relationships across systems, and encodes the business rules governing what an agent is permitted to do. Without that contextual layer, there is no single source of truth — only a larger warehouse of conflicting data, and an AI agent with the keys to act on it. Consider an AI agent tasked with resolving a delayed customer order. To complete the task, it must: To choose the right action, the agent needs a current, unified view of the customer, order, and related records, along with the business rules that govern its response. Delivering that context requires a real-time, unified data product. This is an ongoing discipline, not a one-time cleanup: Identities, relationships, and rules must stay current as records change and new information arrives. Giving agents relevant, reconciled context can also reduce token consumption by limiting the need to retrieve and compare conflicting records. Forrester's research identifies context management and error recovery as sources of AI agent failure, underscoring that fixes focused on prompts or model tuning are insufficient. Enterprises must address the quality and reliability of the context their agents use to act. They must also break down the wall between analytical and operational data. Autonomous agents need to reason across historical patterns and real-time operational state simultaneously, without sacrificing governance or speed. The foundational models powering AI agents will continue to commoditize. Within a few years, the raw model capabilities available to competing enterprises will look virtually identical. [Editors](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-team/) have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: fact-checked preprint trusted source proofread ![KAIST cuts AI fine-tuning from 10 hours to 3… faster development of medical and coding AI](https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/800a/2026/kaist-cuts-ai-fine-tun.jpg "Conceptual diagram of the clustering-based balanced data sampling and allocation method developed by the research team. Different colors represent clusters of data that have similar effects on learning, and different shapes within the same color represent specific data types within each cluster. In conventional training on the full data set, data types with a large number of samples can be repeatedly included across multiple GPUs, so similar computations may be repeated. The proposed method selects diverse data from each cluster in a balanced way and allocates different clusters to each GPU, which reduces redundant computation. Credit: KAIST") Can AI fine-tuning that once took 10 hours be completed in just three hours? KAIST researchers have developed a technology that selects the most useful training data and distributes it evenly across multiple GPUs. By reducing repetitive learning of similar data, the method shortened training time by up to 69.6% while maintaining nearly the same AI performance. The technology is expected to help develop AI tailored to specific tasks, such as corporate customer service or assisting medical professionals with information retrieval, more quickly and at lower cost. A research team led by professor Jae-Gil Lee from the School of Computing developed "CluSTER," a large language model fine-tuning technology that groups and selects data with similar effects on learning and distributes them evenly across multiple GPUs. The research findings were presented in October 2026 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026) and are available on the *arXiv* preprint server. Hyunjin Kim, a doctoral student in the KAIST School of Computing, participated in the [study](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.12584) as the first author, with Lee as the corresponding author. Youngeun Nam, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Toronto, and Jaemin Han and Wonhyeok Choi, master's students at the KAIST Graduate School of Data Science, participated as co-authors. ## Random allocation repeats similar learning A large language model must be trained further on relevant data before it can be used in a specific field such as coding or medicine. This process is called "fine-tuning." It is similar to teaching a broadly knowledgeable AI coding problems and solutions or medical questions and answers so that it can perform tasks in that particular field more effectively. This process requires substantial computation, so multiple GPUs divide the data and process it in parallel. Currently fundraising on [Wefunder](https://wefunder.com/riecomp), the company is pursuing an ecosystem that combines publicly accessible AI projects with proprietary enterprise technologies. Led by founder Andrew Magdy Kamal, Riemann Computing aims to expand who can build, train and customize AI—not merely who can use it. Through its OpenPeer AI initiative, the company is exploring decentralized infrastructure and alternative training approaches intended to give individual developers, researchers and smaller organizations greater opportunities to participate. A central example is the “My Name is Riemann” prerelease language model with approximately 13.1 billion parameters. Developed from published OpenPeerLLM weights through staged model growth, the project uses the OpenPeer-AI-NTK-Trainer to explore a more resource-conscious approach to continued model development. According to company-provided figures, the project used approximately $3,000 worth of local hardware during its initial training phase, followed by roughly $640 in cloud computing. The company reports that those subsequent stages ran on a DigitalOcean node equipped with eight AMD MI325X GPUs for 21 node-hours, equivalent to 168 GPU-hours. These figures describe reported hardware and cloud resources, not a comprehensive accounting of labor, research, data preparation or prior model development. The prerelease is an early demonstration rather than a production-ready chatbot or evidence of performance equivalent to leading frontier models. Riemann Computing intends it to provide a foundation for further training, experimentation and application development. That vision extends beyond AI models. Founded in 2018 and formerly known as Stark Drones Corporation, Riemann Computing develops technologies spanning data compression, computing and decentralized infrastructure. Alongside its accessible AI projects, the company plans to commercialize and sell proprietary codecs, enterprise models and systems. By connecting infrastructure efficiency with broader developer participation, Riemann Computing hopes to help creators play a larger role in shaping AI’s future. Prospective supporters can review the company’s fundraising campaign at <https://wefunder.com/riecomp>, including offering terms and risk disclosures. In experiments, a 109-million-parameter text JEPA scored 0.184 on a cross-modal representation alignment metric, above the 72-billion-parameter Qwen2.5 and the 70-billion-parameter Llama-3. Models trained with the new approach needed only 21.6 million samples to reach the alignment level that next-token-prediction models achieved with 900 million samples—a sample-efficiency gap of roughly 42x. The researchers stress that the result applies only to representation alignment and does not mean small models are stronger at general tasks such as reasoning and coding. ##### Key Elements ![A 109-Million-Parameter Model Outperforms a 72-Billion-Parameter Giant: LeCun's Team Poses a Challenge to the ](https://img.biggo.com/R1gNwCxp4hfEwEbx1K52zFvAa1ITnvf2tKHVkckpNQM/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTExLzZhYjk3MzVmLTA1MWMtNDQ3My05MmQ1LTA5YmZlMTZjMTllNF8xNzkzNjczMDQ1X2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) A text model with just 109 million parameters scored 0.184 on a cross-modal representation alignment test, beating the 72-billion-parameter Qwen2.5 (0.154) and the 70-billion-parameter Llama-3 (0.151). That is a parameter gap of roughly 660x—and the small model came out ahead. The research, by Yann LeCun and Randall Balestriero, an assistant professor of computer science at Brown University, was released as a paper on October 29 titled "Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs." The question the paper tackles is more fundamental than "how big should models be": when AI observes the world through images and through text, what determines whether it can form similar internal understandings? The team's conclusion is that what a model is taught to learn during training matters more than simply making it bigger. **From hypothesis to theorem** The starting point is the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH), proposed at ICML 2024 by MIT and other institutions. The hypothesis observed that as capabilities grow, the internal representations of image models and language models appear to converge—a photo of a cat on a couch and a sentence describing the same scene have completely different input forms but point to the same real-world object. But the hypothesis rested only on empirical curves and intuitive arguments, with neither a mathematical proof nor an actionable training recipe. LeCun and Balestriero's approach treats different modalities as observations of the same underlying world state and asks under what conditions models can learn representations that align with each other. The answer lies in how training samples are constructed. The paper distinguishes two types of data relationships. One is called "Good Views"—different valid observations of the same scene, such as two different text descriptions of the same image, where wording and sentence structure can vary but the subjects and relationships in the scene remain broadly consistent. The other is called "Bad Views"—for example, a prefix and its continuation within the same passage, or fragments obtained by masking the same input. The scheme targets startups founded within the past five years that have raised less than USD $15 million. Participants will receive 12 months of free access to Firefly Pro Plus, Acrobat Studio, which includes Adobe Express Premium, and Semrush. Adobe is positioning the offer around branding, content creation and customer acquisition at a stage when founders are often handling design, marketing and sales themselves. Alongside software access, the programme includes workshops and other opportunities to learn from Adobe specialists and connect with other founders. **What is included** Firefly Pro Plus is Adobe's generative AI product for image, video and audio work. Acrobat Studio combines PDF tools, Adobe's AI Assistant and Adobe Express, while Semrush adds search and marketing data intended to show how a business appears online across both conventional and AI-led search. The package is designed to bring together content creation, document tools and marketing support in one programme for small teams. Adobe serves a wide range of customers, from individual creators and small businesses to large corporate users. The launch comes as software groups seek to embed AI more deeply into products aimed at smaller businesses and startup teams, which often work with limited budgets and staff. For early-stage companies, branding and customer communication can be difficult to prioritise when product development and fundraising take precedence. **Startup examples** Adobe highlighted several startup users as examples of the businesses it wants to reach through the programme. DataCurve, which works on fan identity and intelligence for sports, media and entertainment organisations, already uses Firefly for creative work and sees broader potential for Adobe tools in linking customer data with content creation. "Creativity is far more powerful when you understand who you're creating for. We already use Adobe Firefly for creative assets, and we see an even bigger opportunity to bring DataCurve's fan intelligence directly into the creative process. Imagine a global soccer club creating content that evolves throughout the season as it learns more about what each fan cares about. Adobe for Startups gives us the tools to start bringing that vision to life," said Aman Johar, Co-founder and CEO of DataCurve. Gondola, which is building a digital credit and portfolio system for the social media and digital content sector, said Adobe's products have been part of its workflow since the company's earliest stages. "Adobe has been part of how we work from day one. When you're launching a company, how you show up matters as much as what you build. These enhanced capabilities will help us drive sustainable growth, improve productivity, and support margin expansion, creating capacity to reinvest into our enterprise to serve our consumers.” **[Read more:** [**What trends will drive beauty sales?**](https://drugstorenews.com/what-trends-will-drive-beauty-sales)**]** The cosmetics company will also harness Microsoft technology to advance its Unified Data Platform, which serves a foundation for connecting its data across brands, regions, channels, and functions to reduce duplication, enable reusable data products, and create more consistent access to data-driven insights. AI Product.content: # Nine Bay Area Venture Capital Firms Launch New Funds in October, Targeting AI, Robotics and Deep Tech ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Bay-Area-VC-Firms-Launch-New-Funds.png) Venture capital firms in the San Francisco Bay Area raised millions of dollars in new capital in October 2026, *according to* [*Ivelina Dineva*](https://lnkd.in/p/gD9u-6ne)*, founder of* [*EverythingStartups*](https://www.linkedin.com/company/everythingstartups/home/), reflecting investor interest in artificial intelligence, enterprise software, robotics, deep technology and global startup markets. Nine firms, including Bison Ventures, Endeavor Catalyst, Anorak Ventures and Headline, announced new funds or fundraising milestones during the period, with vehicles ranging from $11.3 million to $400 million. Their investment strategies reveal a venture market increasingly focused on backing AI-driven businesses, developing physical-world technologies and helping early-stage companies turn technical innovation into commercially viable enterprises. ![](https://www.citybiz.co/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Ivelina-Dineva.png) ###### Founder ### Ivelina Dineva [Connect »](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ivelina-dineva-nft/) ###### Company ### EverythingStartups [Learn More »](https://www.everythingstartups.com/) **Here is a snapshot of the nine firms**: [**49 Palms Ventures**](https://www.linkedin.com/company/49palmsvc/home/)**: A $100 Million Fund Focused on AI Startups and Monetization** PALO ALTO, CALIFORNIA 49 Palms Ventures is building its investment strategy around a problem that is becoming increasingly important for artificial intelligence startups: turning technical capabilities into sustainable revenue. The firm invests in early-stage AI companies and combines capital with advice on pricing, commercial contracts and enterprise sales. Its approach reflects the challenges facing AI founders as they move beyond initial product demonstrations and attempt to establish recurring, economically viable businesses. Founded by [Madhavan Ramanujam](https://www.linkedin.com/in/madhavansf/) and [Josh Bloom](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jbloom49/), the firm draws on the founders’ experience advising companies on pricing and monetization. Their investment thesis centers on helping startups establish commercial models early, including usage-based, outcome-based and hybrid pricing structures. As AI companies face questions about inference costs, including customer acquisition, and the economics of delivering increasingly sophisticated services, the firm’s investment thesis shows that a product that attracts early enterprise interest may still struggle to generate attractive margins if its pricing does not account for infrastructure and deployment costs. 49 Palms says its team has worked with more than 500 companies and 100 unicorns as an investor and adviser to AI founders, with a focus on commercial strategy alongside financing. The firm prioritizes monetization. For founders developing AI applications, enterprise software and infrastructure, that expertise could help bridge the gap between product development and commercial adoption. The venture firm invests in businesses using scientific research and engineering breakthroughs to create new products and markets. Its investment strategy targets technologies that require substantial technical development and may take longer to reach commercial scale than conventional software businesses. AI Product.content: IT Brief Asia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [Powered By](https://techday.asia) [Data Protection](https://itbrief.asia/tag/data-protection) [SIEM](https://itbrief.asia/tag/security-information-and-event-management) [Cloud Security](https://itbrief.asia/tag/cloud-security) # CrowdStrike & Dell launch AI Factory security package Tue, 3rd Nov 2026 (Today) [MARA SUGUE News Editor](/author/mara-sugue) CrowdStrike and Dell Technologies have launched an integrated security offering for the Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA. The arrangement lets customers buy CrowdStrike security tools alongside Dell AI infrastructure and services within the Dell AI ecosystem. It is intended to protect enterprise AI systems across infrastructure, workloads, agents and applications. CrowdStrike's Falcon platform will be used with Dell's AI infrastructure and NVIDIA computing systems. Customers in Dell Technologies' AI Ecosystem Program can buy the combined package in line with NVIDIA's AI Factory reference architecture. Dell's Managed Detection and Response service will also expand to manage the CrowdStrike tools within the Dell AI Factory environment. **Security layers** The offering includes three CrowdStrike products. Falcon Guardian is aimed at AI agents and applications, including monitoring agent activity and protecting against prompt injection, malicious behaviour and exposure of sensitive data. Falcon Cloud Security is designed to protect AI infrastructure and workloads from development through runtime. It is intended to identify misconfigurations and vulnerabilities, detect threats, and secure workloads across containers and Kubernetes environments. Falcon Next-Gen SIEM is positioned as the operational layer, bringing together data from CrowdStrike and third-party sources for detection, investigation and response. The integration also builds on NVIDIA OpenShell. Support extends to NVIDIA OpenShell secure runtime, while further integrations with NVIDIA Sentry and NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs are planned. Dell's Managed Detection and Response service will provide round-the-clock monitoring, investigation and response across the AI stack. It will manage the CrowdStrike tools exclusively within this environment. **Executive comments** George Kurtz, Chief Executive Officer and Founder of CrowdStrike, framed the launch as a response to the security risks that accompany rapid AI adoption. "Every enterprise is racing to build AI, but AI without security is an opportunity for the adversary. Security cannot be an afterthought in an AI-powered world. Dell and NVIDIA are powering the AI revolution, and CrowdStrike is securing it. Together, we're making Falcon's AI-native protection foundational to the AI Factory, giving enterprises the confidence to safely innovate at scale on validated, optimised architectures," said Kurtz. Michael Dell, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Dell Technologies, said customers want to adopt AI quickly without increasing risk. "Enterprises are under real pressure to move fast on AI, but speed without security creates risk, not value. The Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA gives customers a validated, optimised foundation, and with CrowdStrike's AI-native security integrated from the start, they can move forward with confidence. That's how you give organisations a clear, trusted path from AI ambition to AI outcomes," said Dell. Jensen Huang, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of NVIDIA, said the move reflects the growing role of AI agents in business operations. "AI agents are transforming how every company works, and capability and security must advance together. CrowdStrike is bringing its cybersecurity platform to the Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA and extending support to NVIDIA OpenShell. Together, we're helping enterprises protect the infrastructure that runs AI and the agents that act on their behalf, giving them the confidence to put AI to work across their business," said Huang. Version 0.37 of [LLM](/dossier/llm), the command-line tool and Python library, is now available. It introduces new models, a command to add [OpenAI](/dossier/openai)-compatible endpoints, and an evolution of embeddings. The maintainer also details how they manage the influx of AI-assisted pull requests. ## Twelve Corrections Integrated and AI-Assisted Sorting Version 0.37 of [LLM](/glossaire/llm) incorporates corrections proposed by 12 authors, most of whom the maintainer indicates were assisted by AI. They specify that the review workload was less than expected and that they treat these proposals as bug reports accompanied by examples, sometimes accepting them or applying their own corrections. To sort these contributions, they rely on Opus 5.5 or [GPT](/glossaire/gpt)-6 Astra to identify the most useful fixes. While many open-source project maintainers report an influx of AI-generated pull requests, the LLM lead believes their project is the most affected among theirs, without it being a problem. Twelve contributors are explicitly thanked for this version: 0d00ciallo0721, ac1982, Allen Flux, Bian Yuhan, Bishop Kammeraad, Chen Yufeiyang, Christopher Krah, Ethan Stoner, Jiachen Xie, Olamide Faniyan, Sharat Chandra Sai Boddu, and nosmile99. A new command, llm openai endpoint add, simplifies the configuration of additional models via OpenAI-compatible endpoints. ## New Default Model and More Flexible Embeddings The default model is now gpt-6-luna, which is priced at half that of the previous default model, gpt-5.6-luna. Open Source AI.content: ![Georgia Institute of Technology](/legacy/image.php?image=https://media.newswise.com/institutions/7008/GTOneLine_TechGold20211012131057.png) # Researchers Create Tool to Detect AI-Hallucinated Legal Citations 2-Nov-2026 at 10:50 AM EST, by [Georgia Institute of Technology](/institutions/newsroom/7008/) [*♡*](/users/login/?ret=%2Farticles%2Fresearchers-create-tool-to-detect-ai-hallucinated-legal-citations%2F%3Fad2f%3D1%26aid%3D857755 "Add to Favorites") [![Newswise: Researchers Create Tool to Detect AI-Hallucinated Legal Citations](/legacy/image.php?image=aHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzLnJlc2VhcmNoLmdhdGVjaC5lZHUvc2l0ZXMvZGVmYXVsdC9maWxlcy9zdHlsZXMvd2lkZS9wdWJsaWMvbmV3cy8yMDI2LTEwL0Fkb2JlU3RvY2tfMmNjMGRhZTUtYTkzYy00MmIyLWJmMzAtNDE5MTY2YWE4ZjBiLmpwZy53ZWJwP2l0b2s9M200MFltY3o=)](/articles/media-article/857755 "View full image") Newswise — As more legal documents are drafted with large language models (LLMs), falsified citations are becoming a problem for the people who rely on them. Georgia Tech researchers have created a tool to help lawyers verify their work. Through a donation from IBM, Georgia Tech’s Center for Scientific Software Engineering (CSSE) and Open Source Program Office (OSPO) held a fellowship competition for students to work with mentors at CSSE and OSPO to create the tool. Master’s students [**Adrian Lozada**](https://adrian123l.github.io/) and [**Di Wu**](https://woodygoodenough.com/) were selected as fellows to work on the project. [The Mellea Legal Requirements Checker](https://github.com/gt-csse/mellea-lrc/) (Mellea-LRC) can quickly identify and accurately verify case law citations, specifically checking for citations that are hallucinated by artificial intelligence (AI). One fellowship goal was to give lawyers and others in the legal field a tool to easily verify legal citations. Mella-LRC does this by using both LLMs and IBM’s Mellea open-source framework to verify and repair LLM prompts. The team tested the tool on 26 public court-filing documents containing falsified citations. Mellea-LRC can process a document in about eight minutes. The tool first extracts the case law citations from the legal document. It then verifies that each citation is authentic and supports the document's content. “IBM’s Mellea framework was the foundation we built it on. Mellea’s job is to make model calls predictable: you write the rules the output must satisfy as ordinary code, and the framework retries until LLM output meets them. Our job was to leverage the framework to build the legal application from end to end,” Wu said. An important aspect of the project was ensuring the tool’s code was open source. The team supported this goal by also creating and releasing a new test and validation dataset on Hugging Face – a popular open-source AI development community – for future benchmarking studies. “Agentic AI is growing quickly, and much of the growth happens in open-source projects, where anyone can read, use, and improve the work,” Lozada said. OSPO Director and Principal Research Scientist [**Jeff** **Young**](https://jyoung3131.github.io/) noted that IBM’s Mellea framework was critical to this work in that its “instruct, verify, repair” paradigm allows for the creation of reliable LLM loops as well as the use of small language models (SLMs), such as IBM’s Granite, which can be run on a laptop. “This project demonstrates the power of open-source models like IBM Granite as well as the importance of using novel software engineering and algorithmic techniques from the Mellea project to improve the reliability of our existing LLMs and SLMs. “Mellea-LRC provides a compelling example of AI’s potential to evolve from a source of error in the legal profession into a trusted ally by helping lawyers work faster and cite precedents more accurately,” Young said. **Original release:** <https://news.research.gatech.edu/2026/10/30/researchers-create-tool-detect-ai-hallucinated-legal-citations> [Request an Expert](/resources/expert-query?article_id=857755...

At least nine AI development platforms disclosed security incidents during the month, according to cybersecurity company Wiz, which described the series as "Black October." Several attacks targeted credentials that allow users to access powerful AI models, potentially enabling criminals to use expensive computing resources without authorization, resell access or extract information from the models. In some incidents, attackers were suspected of deploying autonomous AI agents capable of identifying vulnerabilities, exploiting systems and expanding their access with limited human intervention. Meanwhile, AI also played a role in defending against cyber threats. Security researchers used advanced models to identify critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language used by millions of websites, and help develop security patches. The incidents extended beyond AI companies, with cryptocurrency exchange Binance suffering an estimated $6.3 billion theft and Japanese video game publisher Capcom reporting unauthorized access affecting nearly 11.8 million customer records. However, the attacks differed in their methods and objectives, and authorities have not established that they were part of a single coordinated campaign or that AI was used in every case. Here is a timeline of major cybersecurity incidents reported in October, beginning with the latest: ### Oct. 29, Binance Hackers compromise hot wallets belonging to Binance, one of the world's largest cryptocurrency exchanges, stealing approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets. Initial investigations point to a compromised employee laptop and additional unauthorized access to internal systems, although the full method of attack remains under investigation. Binance temporarily suspends withdrawals and works with law enforcement and blockchain investigators to trace stolen funds. By Oct. 31, the company says it has replenished approximately 90% of the stolen assets and pledged to cover all customer losses. Although the attack demonstrates the vulnerability of digital financial infrastructure, Binance has not established that AI was used to carry out the intrusion. ### Oct. 29, Polymarket Prediction-market platform Polymarket suffers a security breach after attackers compromise a third-party performance-monitoring script used on its website. The malicious script exploits active user sessions to sell trading positions and transfer funds from affected wallets. Polymarket temporarily suspends trading, removes the compromised script and resets active login sessions. The company announces approximately $3.9 million in repayments and compensation to affected users. The incident highlights the risks posed by third-party software embedded in online platforms, although no specific role for AI in conducting the attack has been established. ### Oct. 29, Cursor Attackers distribute a maliciously modified version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension through the marketplace of Cursor, an AI-powered software development platform. [Founder first](https://yourstory.com/#founder-first) [Just In](https://yourstory.com/search?page=1&tag=Just%2520In) Brands Resources YSTV ![close menu bar](https://images.yourstory.com/cs/images/homepage/headerV3_menu_cross_button.svg?format=auto&w=128&q=75) ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT [Technology](/category/technology) # How the open-source route helped Uzair Ali land global roles ## Open source was not a shortcut for this young techie to land an interview or a job; it was a proactive way to make his work speak for himself. ![Photo of Team YS](https://images.yourstory.com/cs/static/default-ys-image.jpg?format=auto&w=96&q=75)[Team YS](/author/webmaster)[17489 Stories](/author/webmaster) ![How the open-source route helped Uzair Ali land global roles ](https://images.yourstory.com/cs/2/220356402d6d11e9aa979329348d4c3e/Etherealmachines10-1793616466333.png?mode=crop&crop=faces&ar=2%3A1&format=auto&w=1920&q=75) Monday November 02, 2026, 3 min Read [![Google Preferred](https://images.yourstory.com/assets/images/google_preferred.webp?format=auto&w=384&q=75)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=yourstory.com) Indian engineers no longer have to relocate abroad or go through several rounds of resume screening and interviews to bag global roles. Increasingly, open-source public code is paving the way for that. Public code is a record anyone can read and inspect, and hiring teams are actively using it to assess one's real-world engineering skills. It includes open-source contributions, public repositories (like GitHub), and code samples that hiring managers can evaluate. This is how Uzair Ali landed internships at various global companies and eventually became a founding engineer at a US-based fintech startup. As a college student at the Kalinga Institute of Industrial Technology in Bhubaneswar, Ali was building a tool to monitor server logs. He shared his repository of work in open source on X, which caught the attention of the CTO of Dukaan, an Indian mobile-first, do-it-yourself ecommerce platform**,** leading to an interview at the firm. Ali joined Dukaan as a backend intern in January 2022 in Bengaluru. This was an early lesson in the value of making his work visible to the world. It helped his project reach someone who might otherwise have not seen his resume. Ali's career path did not follow a straight line through a typical hiring funnel at big tech companies. After a stint at Dukaan, he interned at HackerRank and FamPay while still being in university. After graduating, he joined Civo, a London-based cloud infrastructure provider. Twenty-four-year-old Ali is now an engineer at Flip Laboratories, a San Francisco-based fintech startup. He works from India. In an interaction with *YourStory*, Ali says all his career moves from being a backend engineer to AI work and now to being part of the founding team at Flip are largely thanks to his open-source contributions. Ali reasons that open-source code helps software maintainers see how people works over months, while the reviews show how they handle feedback. Now anyone with an internet connection can pick a project, fix what is broken, and receive feedback and reviews. Over time, this history builds a credible repository of one's work in a way a resume cannot, says the techie. Ali's GitHub profile has a number of pull requests merged in various open source projects such as LiteLLM, a widely used open-source LLM gateway. A pull request is a request from others to merge a code into their projects, and this is reveiwed jointly by those who create the code and those who would like to integrate it. Ali's most visible work is on Agno, an open-source framework for building AI agents. It has more than 42,000 stars on GitHub. He also has contributions in major codebases including Terraform, Crossplane, and IntelOwl. It’s an argument Qualcomm made in July when first pitching the HBC architecture, and one they continue to make now. “In traditional computer architecture, you usually have DDR, you have memory of package, you have usually plenty of capacity on that, but you have a narrow link, which moves the data very slowly,” Gerardo Giaretta, vice president and general manager of datacenter CPU and AI at Qualcomm, recently told journalists and analysts. “So far, AI has been really focusing on the HBM architecture. Infra & Chips.content: الحساب الاقسام ## آخر الأخبار # Marvell to buy Lumentum in $115 billion deal in AI data-center bet ![9847cf53-f92e-461b-8c84-a981a27ba8dc.jpg](https://twaslnews1.twaslnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/9847cf53-f92e-461b-8c84-a981a27ba8dc.jpg) By Anhata RoopraiNov 2 (Reuters) – Marvell Technology is buying optical components maker Lumentum in a $115 billion all-stock deal, including debt, as the custom chipmaker takes on larger rival Broadcom in a race to cash in on the AI spending boom.The deal, announced on Monday, is one of the biggest in 2026 and among the boldest bets yet on the AI build-out that chip executives expect to underpin industry demand for years.The heavy spending, however, is also facing a major reality check as investors begin to doubt its sustainability in the face tightening margins and slowing cash flow, triggering a selloff in chip stocks. “AI infrastructure is undergoing a fundamental architectural shift toward optical connectivity, creating an opportunity that comes along once in a generation,” said Marvell CEO Matt Murphy, who will remain chairman and CEO of the combined company.”We intend to help shape the next era of AI connectivity and create exceptional stockholder value.”Lumentum shares fell 1.5% before the bell, while Marvell was down 0.7%. Both stocks have fallen sharply since deal talks were first reported late last month due to the AI bubble concerns.By buying Lumentum – a company roughly half its size – Marvell is betting that Big Tech’s AI spending boom is here to stay and would keep demand for optical components used to move data at high speeds outstripping supply.Lumentum makes photonic products, including high-performance lasers and optical components used in AI, cloud computing and communications networks.AI chip giant Nvidia, which invested $2 billion each in Marvell and Lumentum earlier this year, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the deal. Just three years ago, Marvell was a relatively little-known chipmaker. But its market value has since surged to more than $170 billion, thanks to its role in helping tech giants such as Amazon develop custom AI chips and networking technology for data centers.”Combining Marvell’s custom chips and networking expertise with Lumentum’s optical components could give it a much stronger hand as data centres demand ever-faster, more energy-efficient connections,” said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG Group.”But this is an enormous bet, and investors are right to ask whether Marvell is paying too much and taking on too much at once.” Monday’s deal could also add more muscle to Marvell in its race with rival Broadcom, which has long been Alphabet-owned Google’s main custom-chip partner and offers customers a broader menu of AI data center hardware under one roof. AdvertisementMarvell notched one of its biggest wins in August, signing a deal to supply chips that sit alongside Google’s AI processors worth up to $120 billion in sales through fiscal 2033, giving the search giant the right to buy a $12.2 billion stake.At its investor day in October, Marvell forecast fiscal 2031 sales of $70 billion to $90 billion. It expects around $37.5 billion of that to come from interconnect, a market it expects to grow 65% a year to $65 billion by 2030.HOW THE DEAL IS STRUCTUREDUnder Monday’s agreement, Marvell will pay $1,132 per share in stock, a 23.9% premium to Lumentum’s last unaffected closing price on October 28, before deal talks were first reported.That gives the deal an equity value of $102.54 billion.Marvell said the acquisition would expand the combined company’s total addressable market to $550 billion.Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share they own, giving them roughly 33% ownership of the combined company on a fully diluted basis.The transaction was unanimously approved by the boards of both companies and is expected to close in the first half of calendar 2028.LUMENTUM MAY BENEFIT FROM PRO...

Infra & Chips.content: # From capacity, to the cost of intelligence Amit Agrawal, President, Techno Digital The next shift in AI infrastructure We are already in an era where intelligence comes with a price tag. Every answer, inference, agent, and AI workflow carries a real infrastructure cost, and that cost isn't determined by the model alone. It rises or falls with compute efficiency, utilization, power, cooling, networking, latency, and workload architecture. The same intelligence can have radically different economics depending on where, when, and how it is delivered. Back in March 2023, running a GPT-4-class model cost roughly $20 per million tokens. Today, that same intelligence costs less than $0.50, a fall of nearly 98 percent in three years. Yet the average enterprise AI budget has grown nearly six times over the same period, from $1.2 million in 2024 to approximately $7 million in 2026. Intelligence has never been cheaper. AI has never cost more. Unit price is falling while total spend rises. That is the paradox defining AI infrastructure in 2026, and it is why the industry’s most important conversation is shifting from how much capacity we can build to how much usable intelligence that capacity can deliver, per dollar, per watt, and per second. What follows is the case for that shift: the economics behind it, the chips accelerating it, and the power constraint quietly capping it. ## From capacity to productivity The first phase of the AI infrastructure race was necessarily about capacity. Compute was scarce, demand was accelerating, and hyperscalers, enterprises, and governments moved quickly to secure GPUs, power, and data center capacity. That capacity remains essential, but it doesn't by itself determine AI economics. A GPU cluster running at high utilization has very different unit economics from the same cluster sitting partially idle. The question is evolving from how much compute is available to how productively that compute converts into usable intelligence. Earlier this year, a widely circulated figure claimed DeepSeek had trained a frontier model for just $5.6 million. That number actually referred to pre-training compute for an earlier model, not the total cost of the frontier model itself, a distinction lost in the headlines. Weeks later, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, and Google all reaffirmed or increased their AI capex guidance rather than cutting it. This is Jevons’ paradox in action: when efficiency gains lower the price of a resource, total consumption tends to rise, not fall. Every dollar saved per token becomes the reason to run ten more tokens in parallel, not the reason to build less. ## The price of a GPU is not the cost of intelligence Nvidia’s own Blackwell-vs-Hopper analysis illustrates the distinction. While newer-generation infrastructure can carry a higher GPU-hour cost, its delivered cost per million tokens can be substantially lower because of gains in throughput, memory, interconnect, software optimization, and energy efficiency. Buyers evaluating AI infrastructure on hardware price or theoretical compute performance alone are therefore optimizing for an incomplete metric. The true cost of intelligence is determined by the entire stack. Model efficiency determines how much computation an output requires. Compute architecture determines how efficiently accelerators, memory, and interconnects execute the workload. Utilization determines how much installed infrastructure is doing productive work rather than sitting idle. Infrastructure efficiency determines how effectively power and cooling support high-density compute. And workload placement determines the latency, network, and data-movement economics of where intelligence is produced and consumed. Optimizing any one layer in isolation can produce misleading economics. A highly efficient model running on poorly utilized infrastructure can still be expensive. Infra & Chips.content: [Skip to content](#content) # Marvell Buys Lumentum for $115 Billion in the Biggest Chip Deal of the A.I. Era ![Avatar](https://www.trendingtopics.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Trendy_AI-150x150.webp)[co-produced by AI](https://www.trendingtopics.eu/author/trendy-ai/ "Posts by co-produced by AI"), ![Avatar](https://www.trendingtopics.eu/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/11741112_10152626834202824_6426697770492090456_o-150x150.jpg)[Jakob Steinschaden](https://www.trendingtopics.eu/author/jakob/ "Posts by Jakob Steinschaden") ![](https://www.trendingtopics.eu/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/marvell-custom-asic-ki-chip-780x436.webp) © Marvell [Set Trending Topics as a preferred source on Google.](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=trendingtopics.eu) Marvell is paying $115 billion for a company most people have never heard of, and the market is sending both stocks down. U.S. chip designer Marvell Technology is acquiring photonics specialist Lumentum in an all-stock transaction. Lumentum shareholders receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each of their shares, which works out to about $1,132 (about €974) per share, a premium of 23.9 percent over the price before the first takeover rumors. Including debt, the deal values Lumentum at $115 billion (about €99 billion), with an equity value of $102.5 billion. After closing, Marvell shareholders will hold about 67 percent of the combined company and Lumentum’s about 33 percent. Both boards approved the deal unanimously; Marvell chief Matt Murphy stays on as chairman and CEO, and Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston joins the Marvell board along with two other directors. The transaction is not expected to close until the first half of 2028, pending approval by shareholders and antitrust authorities. For scale: Broadcom paid $69 billion for VMware in 2023, Dell paid $67 billion for EMC in 2016, and the largest chip takeover ever attempted, Broadcom’s $130 billion bid for Qualcomm, was blocked by the U.S. government in 2018. Marvell and Lumentum call it one of the biggest tech deals ever; according to Bloomberg, it is the year’s largest merger by equity value.
